LOS ANGELES (AP) — Susan Saint James, who co-starred with Rock Hudson in the 1970s TV crime series “McMillan & Wife” and later co-starred with Jane Curtin in the sitcom “Kate & Allie” in the 1980s, has died. She was 80.

People magazine, citing a representative for the actor, said Saint James died Monday. She had been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

“She never met a stranger,” her family said in a statement to People. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.”

Born Susan Jane Miller on Aug. 14, 1946, in Los Angeles, she was raised in the northern Illinois city of Rockford, where her father had transferred for work. She began modeling as a teenager in Paris.

At 20, she moved back to Los Angeles and landed a seven-year contract with Universal Studios. She made her television debut in the 1966 movie “Fame is the Name of the Game” with Tony Franciosa.

She got another break when it became a series called “The Name of the Game” in 1968, with rotating lead characters played by Franciosa, Gene Barry and Robert Stack. Saint James provided the show continuity in her role as Peggy Maxwell, a research assistant who worked for all three men. She won an Emmy Award for the part in 1969.

Before “The Name of the Game,” Saint James had a recurring role in the crime-caper series “It Takes a Thief” starring Robert Wagner. Her other early TV credits included “Ironside,” “McCloud” and “Alias Smith and Jones.” In 1980, she guest-starred in an episode of “M(asterisk)A(asterisk)S(asterisk)H.”

Saint James, known for her unique, throaty voice, had a supporting role in the 1968 movie “Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows” starring Rosalind Russell and Stella Stevens.

Breakout role in ‘McMillan & Wife’

She earned her biggest fame as Sally McMillan, the plucky wife of Hudson’s San Francisco police commissioner Stewart McMillan, in the hit series “McMillan & Wife” from 1971-76. She received three Emmy nominations for the role.

Saint James left the NBC show before its sixth and final season because of a contract dispute, with her character killed off in a plane crash. Saint James then turned to feature films.

She played opposite Peter Fonda in “Outlaw Blues” in 1977. She co-starred with George Hamilton in the 1979 vampire spoof “Love at First Bite” and joined Jessica Lange and Curtin in the 1980 comedy heist “How to Beat the High Cost of Living.” She co-starred in the 1981 romantic comedy “Carbon Copy,” in which Denzel Washington made his movie debut.

After middling success on the big screen, Saint James reunited with Curtin in the CBS sitcom “Kate & Allie,” which ran from 1984-89 and earned Saint James two Emmy nominations as the free-spirited Kate to Curtin’s straight-laced Allie.

While guest-hosting “Saturday Night Live” in 1981, Saint James met Dick Ebersol, the show’s then-executive producer and the future chairman of NBC Sports. They married barely six weeks after meeting and had three sons, Charlie, Willie and Teddy.

Teddy died at age 14 in a 2004 private plane crash that also killed the pilot and flight attendant; Ebersol and Charlie survived with serious injuries.

The family had spent Thanksgiving in Los Angeles and were due to make multiple stops on the return trip. The flight landed first in Colorado, where Saint James got off to go to the family’s second home. It crashed upon taking off again for Indiana in snowy weather.

Her family’s statement mentions the loss: “Her defining act: weeks after losing her youngest son, Teddy, in the Nov. 28, 2004 plane crash, she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first.”

Saint James filed for divorce from Ebersol in 2002, but they reconciled later that year. “We had a second chance,” she told People magazine in 2002. “I’m amazingly happier, so that’s a good sign.”

In his 2022 memoir “From Saturday Night to Sunday Night,” Ebersol called Saint James “the greatest partner I’ve ever had by far.”

After ‘Kate & Allie’

She retired when “Kate & Allie” ended, choosing to focus on raising her younger children in Litchfield, Connecticut, while Ebersol took the executive job at NBC Sports.

Saint James made occasional guest appearances after that, including as the mother of her real-life look-alike niece Christa Miller on “The Drew Carey Show,” as well as “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Suits.” In 1999, she starred in a production of “The Miracle Worker” in Torrington, Connecticut.

In 1998, Saint James, her sister, Mercedes Dewey, and a friend founded Seedling and Pip, a baby gift basket business with a focus on books based in Litchfield, Connecticut.

She was a longtime supporter of Special Olympics, volunteering and serving on its board of directors.

Besides her husband, she is survived by daughter Sunshine and son Harmony from her second marriage to makeup artist Tom Lucas, with whom she remained friends; sons Charlie and Willie with Ebersol; and Miller, whose first TV role was on “Kate & Allie.” Saint James’ first marriage to Richard Neubert ended in divorce.

Neil Sedaka

Neil Sedaka, the singer-songwriter behind dozens of hits such as “Breaking Up Is Hard to Do” and “Laugher in the Rain,” died on February 27, 2026. He was 86. Sedaka teamed with lyricist Howard Greenfield on songs that reflected the teen innocence of the post-Elvis/pre-Beatles era of the late 1950s-early 1960s, including “Happy Birthday Sweet Sixteen,” “Calendar Girl” and “Oh! Carol.”

Robert Carradine

Robert Carradine, the "Revenge of the Nerds" star who hailed from one of Hollywood's prominent acting families, died on February 23, 2026. He was 71. Carradine earned a generation of new fans by playing the father in “Lizzie McGuire” and also had a prominent role in the Oscar-decorated “Coming Home” (1978) and appeared in Quentin Tarantino’s “Django Unchained” (2012).

Eric Dane

Eric Dane, the actor best known for his roles on “Grey’s Anatomy” and “Euphoria” and who later in life became an advocate for ALS awareness, died on February 19, 2026. He was 53. Dane developed a devoted fanbase when he was cast as Dr. Mark Sloan, aka McSteamy, on the ABC medical drama “Grey’s Anatomy,” a role he would play from 2006 until 2012 and reprise in 2021. In April 2025, Dane announced he had been diagnosed with ALS, a progressive disease that attacks nerve cells controlling muscles throughout the body.

Jesse Jackson

Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, whose two presidential runs in the 1980s set the stage for today’s progressive movement, died on February 17, 2026. He was 84.

He participated in marches from Selma to Montgomery in Alabama and established a branch of the Martin Luther King Jr.-led Southern Christian Leadership Conference in Chicago. He was later appointed to lead SCLC’s economic arm, Operation Breadbasket.

Robert Duvall

Robert Duvall, an acclaimed and prolific actor celebrated for his complex, rugged roles in films like “The Godfather,” died on February 15, 2026. He was 95. Duvall’s career spanned six decades, during which he accumulated many directing, producing and acting credits. He continued to work until late in his life, acting alongside Martin Sheen in 2021’s “12 Mighty Orphans,” a film about a football team at an orphanage in 1930s Texas, and appearing in 2002’s “Hustle.”

James Van Der Beek

James Van Der Beek, star of the iconic teen drama series "Dawson’s Creek" in the late ’90s and early 2000s, died on February 11, 2026. He was 48. Van Der Beek had announced in November 2024 that he was diagnosed with colorectal cancer.

He participated in theater in middle school, and at 16, he made his professional debut off-Broadway in Edward Albee’s “Finding The Sun.” The next year, he made his feature film debut in the coming-of-age comedy “Angus.” He also starred in “Mercy,” “CSI: Cyber” and most recently “Overcompensating.” His film credits include “Varsity Blues,” “Bad Hair” and “The Rules of Attraction.”

Terrance Gore

Terrance Gore, who was part of World Series championship teams as a speedy bench weapon, died on February 6, 2026. He was 34. He played in 11 postseason games as a pinch runner, stealing five bases in six attempts and scoring three runs. He was a part of a championship team with the Royals (2015), who drafted him with a 20th-round selection in 2011, the Los Angeles Dodgers (2020) and the Atlanta Braves (2021).

Sonny Jurgensen

Hall of Fame quarterback Sonny Jurgensen died on February 6, 2026. He was 91. He topped 3,000 yards in a season five times, including twice with Philadelphia, in an era before rules changes opened up NFL offenses. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1983 and remains the only Washington player to wear the No. 9 jersey in a game.

Catherine O'Hara

Beloved comic actor Catherine O'Hara, best known for her roles in “Schitt’s Creek,” “Home Alone,” “Best in Show” and countless other comedies, died on January 30, 2026. O’Hara, a two-time Emmy Award winner, was 71. O’Hara got her start in 1974 performing with The Second City, an improv comedy troupe with an outpost in Toronto, then joined the group’s spinoff production SCTV.

Bob Weir

Veteran rock musician Bob Weir, the Grateful Dead’s rhythm guitarist who helped guide the legendary jam band, died on January 10, 2026. He was 78. It was Weir who sang the verses on the band’s trademark boogie anthem, “Truckin’,” and who wrote such key songs as “Sugar Magnolia,” “Playing in the Band” and “Jack Straw.”

Doug LaMalfa

Republican Doug LaMalfa, a seven-term U.S. representative from California and a reliable vote on Trump’s agenda, died on January 6, 2026. He was 65. LaMalfa was first elected to Congress in 2012 and represented Northern California’s 1st District, along the Oregon border, including Redding and reaching just north of Sacramento.
